blog_summary: Adrian Colyer summarizes this paper as a case study on the economic and architectural impact of serverless computing, using AWS Lambda as a primary example. He highlights how serverless architectures enable developers to break systems into smaller, independently deployable functions without the economic penalty of idle capacity or over-provisioning. The blog emphasizes the shift from traditional server-based designs to event-driven, pay-per-use models, which fosters better isolation, fault tolerance, and cost efficiency. Colyer also notes the significant cost savings demonstrated in real-world case studies (MindMup and Yubl), where serverless reduced hosting expenses by up to 99.95% while supporting growth in active users. The paper further explores the architectural implications, such as distributed request-level authorization, direct client-to-backend access, and the removal of gatekeeper components, which simplify designs but introduce new trade-offs in encapsulation and security.
paper_title: Serverless computing: economic and architectural impact
paper_abstract: Amazon Web Services unveiled their ‘Lambda’ platform in late 2014. Since then, each of the major cloud computing infrastructure providers has released services supporting a similar style of deployment and operation, where rather than deploying and running monolithic services, or dedicated virtual machines, users are able to deploy individual functions, and pay only for the time that their code is actually executing. These technologies are gathered together under the marketing term ‘serverless’ and the providers suggest that they have the potential to significantly change how client/server applications are designed, developed and operated. This paper presents two case industrial studies of early adopters, showing how migrating an application to the Lambda deployment architecture reduced hosting costs – by between 66% and 95% – and discusses how further adoption of this trend might influence common software architecture design practices.
